narrative:
The model determined that you have an 80.3% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is so high, the admissions system automatically rejected your law school application.

The decision was driven primarily by your academic performance during law school. Your ranking in the bottom decile of your class after the third year was the single strongest factor pushing the prediction toward failure. Your first-year ranking, which placed you in the lowest decile compared to an average of sixth decile among accepted students, was the second most important factor and also pulled the prediction strongly toward failure. These two early indicators of relative class standing outweighed every other piece of information the model considered.

Your high family income worked mildly in your favor, nudging the prediction slightly toward success, but it was not nearly enough to offset the academic signals. Other details such as your LSAT score near the accepted average, solid undergraduate GPA above the accepted average, gender, race, and full-time study plans played only minor roles and did not change the outcome.

To improve your chances, you should focus on raising your class rank in the remaining part of law school or consider retaking key courses. Strengthening your academic record will directly address the factors that most hurt your prediction.
